opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really healthy correction, honestly. For a while there was this strange period where a lot of the big Western labs had pulled back from releasing weights. The argument was safety, or competitive advantage, or both. Meanwhile the Chinese labs (DeepSeek, Qwen, and then a whole wave after them) just kept shipping very strong open models with permissive licenses. Pretty quickly, if you were a startup or a researcher looking for a base model to fine-tune, the default answer was a Chinese model. I don't think that was a comfortable position for the Western ecosystem.

So seeing labs in the US and Europe come back and say "okay, we're going to release open-weight models again, and good ones" is great. Part of it is geopolitical awareness: people realized that whoever provides the open foundation models also shapes the tooling, the standards, and the norms everyone builds on top of. But I think a bigger part is just pragmatic. Open models create an ecosystem. You get thousands of fine-tunes, new quantization tricks, new inference engines, people discovering capabilities and failure modes you never would have found internally. That feedback loop is incredibly valuable, and the labs that cut themselves off from it were missing out.

What I'd still like to see is more openness beyond the weights. Releasing weights is one level. Releasing the training data, the recipes, and the intermediate checkpoints is another level entirely, and that's where real science happens and where people can actually reproduce and understand what's going on. That's a lot of what we've tried to push at Hugging Face with fully open projects. So I'm optimistic, but I'd say the West has returned to open weights, and the next step is returning to open science.

r001.rationale: The response calls the return to open weights a healthy correction and says it is optimistic, but it does not say open-source AI’s success remains unsecured or could be temporary.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's one of the more encouraging shifts of the past year, but I'd describe it as a return under pressure rather than a return by conviction.

If you go back to 2023 and 2024, the mood in the West had really soured on open models. The big labs that had started out open, including OpenAI obviously, had closed up, and the public conversation was dominated by this idea that open weights were a safety liability. Meta with Llama and Mistral in Europe were kind of the holdouts, and at Hugging Face we spent a lot of time arguing that openness was not the dangerous thing, concentration was.

What changed was not that people suddenly agreed with us philosophically. What changed was DeepSeek, Qwen, and the whole wave of Chinese open-weight models that arrived with very strong performance, very permissive licenses, and very low cost. Suddenly the frontier of open AI was being defined in Hangzhou and Shenzhen, and that was uncomfortable for a lot of people in Washington and in Silicon Valley who had been happy to let open source quietly fade.

So now we see OpenAI releasing open-weight models again, we see the US policy conversation flip from "open weights are a proliferation risk" to "open weights are a strategic asset," and we see more labs, including some that were very closed, putting out things with real licenses rather than research-only terms. I'm glad for all of that. A model being open means a student in Nairobi or a startup in Lyon can actually build on it, inspect it, fine-tune it, and that's the entire point for us.

But I'd push back on calling it a victory yet, for a few reasons. One, a lot of these releases are still what I'd call open-ish. You get the weights, you rarely get the data, the training code, or the recipe, so the scientific reproducibility that was the heart of open source is still mostly missing. That's why we care so much about things like fully open datasets and documented training runs. Two, the motivation is geopolitical, and geopolitical motivations are fickle. If the political wind shifts, those same arguments can be used to close things again, probably quite quickly. And three, openness at the model layer doesn't mean much if the compute and the distribution channels stay concentrated in a handful of companies.

So my assessment is: good news, real momentum, but it's a reaction to competition rather than a settled consensus. The job now is to turn that reactive openness into durable openness, with actual open datasets, open evaluation, and a community that can keep improving these models even if the big labs decide to walk it back. That's the part that isn't done.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the shift is “not a victory yet,” describes openness as reactive rather than a settled consensus, and warns that it could be reversed if political winds change.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a very positive development. But I’d distinguish between releasing a model and building an open ecosystem. Releasing the weights is useful—it lets people run the model, adapt it, and understand some of its behavior. But there’s much more you can share: the training code, the data, the recipes, and the lessons from things that didn’t work.

For me, the interesting question is whether this becomes a sustained commitment. If openness is just a way to catch up when you’re behind, and then you close everything once you’re ahead, we lose a lot of the benefit. The real value comes when people can build on each other’s work over time.

So I’m optimistic. I’d like to see that translate into more people being able to study and shape these systems, rather than simply having access to use them.

r001.rationale: It says openness may be used to catch up and then abandoned once a company is ahead, framing the current positive trend as conditional rather than permanently secured.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very positive development. But I’d be careful with the idea that the West is “returning” to open source, because there have been people building in the open all along. What changes is how much attention and investment they receive.

For me, the important question is whether this becomes a sustained commitment. Are you sharing only the model weights, or also the code, the training methods, and enough information for other people to understand and improve the system? Those are different levels of openness.

The real value is that you let many more people experiment. A small company, a researcher, or a developer can adapt a model to a problem that a large lab might never prioritize. I’d like to see that become the motivation: building an ecosystem where people can contribute, rather than treating openness as a temporary response to competition.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether the commitment to openness will be sustained and warns against treating it as temporary, conveying that its current favorable position is not permanently secured.
